title: Ali in the house
hook: young Ali, Abu Talib's son, is raised in the Prophet's home

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zayd chose: offered his father's home, he stayed, and was called a son. Your line was: he chose to stay. Who did you thank for choosing you? Day seven hundred twenty.

A hard year comes to Mecca. Ibn Ishaq calls it a severe famine, and says it hit Quraysh badly. One house feels it hard: Abu Talib's. He's the uncle who took in an orphaned nephew years before, gave him a bed and a place at the table. Now Abu Talib has a big family and not enough to feed them. And the nephew, grown now and married to Khadijah, has an idea. Today: Ali in the house.
screen: `A HARD YEAR IN MECCA.` → `ABU TALIB'S HOUSE STRAINS.` → `THE NEPHEW HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: Day seven hundred eleven gave this plan in a sentence. Here it is up close, as Ibn Ishaq tells it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ goes to another uncle, al-Abbas, and says: your brother Abu Talib has a large family, and you can see how hard things are. Let's lighten his load. I'll take one of his sons, you take one. Al-Abbas agrees. They go to Abu Talib together and ask. So two boys change houses that year. Al-Abbas takes Ja'far. The Prophet takes Ali, a small boy, into his home with Khadijah. Under that roof he joins Khadijah, and Zayd, the boy who chose to stay. A household that keeps making room. Ibn Ishaq says Ali stayed with him from then on, and when revelation came, Ali followed him and believed. Later, the paths read Ali's place in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts him among the rightly guided caliphs; Shia tradition holds him to be the Imam after the Prophet. But here he is still a child at Khadijah's table. Ali wasn't an orphan; his father was alive. The man who took him in had been one, though. And in Sahih al-Bukhari, that man says the one who looks after an orphan will be with him in Paradise like this, and he holds up two fingers side by side. The house that raised Ali was run by someone who knew what that care was worth. Raised in that house.
screen: `A PLAN TO LIGHTEN THE LOAD.` · `TWO BOYS CHANGE HOUSES.` · `A HOUSEHOLD THAT MAKES ROOM.` · `TWO FINGERS SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `RAISED IN THAT HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: care for a child not your own. Settle, and breathe. Think of a child in your world who isn't yours. A niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, a child in a family going through a hard year. Or think back to an adult who did that for you when you were small. Hold that child, or that adult, in mind. Then ask one plain question: what would lighten the load? A meal, a ride, an hour, a book, a kind word to a tired parent. If you pray, you can pray for that child by name. The bell holds the time.
Ali in the house. Abu Talib's young son, taken into the Prophet's home in a hard year to ease his father's load, and raised there. Today's word.
Your line: raised in that house. Today, do one small thing to lighten the load for a child, or for the person raising one. Day seven hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Muslims who sponsor or care for orphans often recall the Prophet's ﷺ words about the two fingers side by side, and Ali's upbringing in his home is told when Muslims remember Ali.

fork.setup: famine, and your uncle, who raised you, has more children than he can feed. what do you do?
options: send him what money you can spare.
ask another uncle to join you, and each take a son.
wait for the year to turn.
fork.reveal: he went to al-Abbas, and they each took a son into their homes. Ali came to the house where the Prophet lived.

original.note: Arabic: taking someone into your care and providing for them, the word used for looking after an orphan.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ali was just a cousin.
what it means: in a hard year, two of Abu Talib's sons changed houses, and Ali joined a household that already had room for Zayd.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq gives the famine, the plan with al-Abbas, and says Ali stayed with him until revelation and believed.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the famine; the Prophet and al-Abbas each take a son of Abu Talib; Ali stays with him and believes)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5304 (the one who looks after an orphan, like these two fingers)

notes: Ibn Ishaq says Ali was the first male to believe; the script deliberately says only that he 'followed him and believed', to avoid a precedence claim that tomorrow's or later lessons may treat (and where Sunni sources also name Abu Bakr and Zayd). Keeper may decide to add it.
Ali's age is not given on purpose; reports differ.
Abu Talib's own request ('leave me Aqil') is omitted; confirm the paraphrase of the plan.
Sunni (a rightly guided caliph) and Shia (the Imam after the Prophet) descriptions of Ali stated side by side; confirm fair.
Sahih al-Bukhari 5304: confirm number and that kafil al-yatim is the wording behind 'looks after an orphan'.
Original: كَفَالَة (kafalah) is the noun; the hadith uses kafil. Confirm acceptable as the day's original word.

Editor: day 711 already told the al-Abbas plan and its 'full circle' angle (Abu Talib took him in, now he takes Abu Talib's son), and its myth game used the same Ali fact; the teach now points back to 711 and turns to the two boys, the household that already held Zayd, and the orphan hadith. Fixed the hadith framing (it is about orphans, not 'a child who isn't yours'; Ali was not an orphan). Cut 'nobody calls it repayment', 'there for everything that came next' and 'both look back to this house'; Sunni/Shia lines now say 'tradition'. Replaced the repeated myth item. Co-residence of Zayd and Ali in the household is inferred from the sirah; Keeper to confirm.
Audit: cut the unsourced superlative 'the strain is worst' in Abu Talib's house (Ibn Ishaq says only that he had a large family and the famine hit Quraysh hard).
